newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: UNHCR chief says West must help in new refugee era.
newsitem.headline: UNHCR chief says West must help in new refugee era.

text.p: The U.N. refugee chief has called on the West to come to grips with the changing and increasingly militarised nature of refugee crises and be more ready to deploy troops.

Sadako Ogata, United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees, said the international community was opting for quick-fix solutions rather than responding creatively to the changing face of refugee movements, increasingly caused by internal conflicts.
Her humanitarian agency needed more support from donors to use force to separate military elements from refugees, such as those in eastern Zaire, Ogata said in an interview this week.
"I appeal to the donors and countries of asylum to come in. They've got the military. They have the security," said Ogata, a former professor of international relations from Japan.
Ogata, with a reputation of having a formidable intellect and strong leadership, said the militarisation of refugee camps would increasingly become the pattern.
"The causes of refugees today are by and large internal conflicts. There will always be militants mixed with refugees."

Ogata said the world's reluctance to send in troops to separate Rwandan refugees from militia had complicated the crisis in east Zaire, where renewed warfare between rebels and Zaire's army has again turned the focus on refugees.
Western countries led by the United States abandoned the idea of the force after most of some 1.1 million Rwandan Hutu refugees in Zaire returned home after rebel victories in 1996.
"There is a desire for quick-fix solutions among those donors who do not understand the causes of refugee crises and the solutions to reconciliation," Ogata said.
She said the problems still remained in eastern Zaire with the presence of up to 400,000 Rwandan Hutu refugees who have opted to stay there and are now trapped in a warzone.

UNHCR's core protection mandate was written in 1951 immediately after World War Two and focused more on individuals fleeing persecution in communist countries than on whole communities fleeing ethnic or military conflicts.
"During the Cold War period, refugees were not militarised people and donors were much more resigned to prolonged refugee problems," Ogata said.
"But today, refugees are victims and sometimes the perpetrators of internal conflicts. They flee together with armed elements."

In Eastern Zaire, the UNHR faced a stark dilemma in interpreting its core protection mandate. Many Rwandan Hutus did not flee persecution so much as prosecution for the 1994 genocide of up to a million Tutsis and Hutu moderates.

The number of people UNHCR has been dealing with has spiralled in recent years. The agency now has more than 26 million refugees and displaced people around the world under its wings, the highest numbers being in Africa.

"Some donors say that UNHCR wants to keep the refugees in camps because in that way we can keep our jobs. That I categorically reject," Ogata said. "We have enough work. We don't need more. We're not here to produce refugees."
UNHCR is also under increasing pressure to find solutions to the problems of refugees when they return home.
"The donors think that if fighting is finished in countries of origin, refugees can go back. They are much less patient."

"Nowadays, we have more responsibility in helping returnees than we thought in the old days," she said. "We try to even create conditions in home countries. We have to ask for patience. It's not just a question of when the fighting ends. Behind this fighting there is a very strong sense of mistrust."
